That is refused here, naming both classes. An EMPTY value is a real key meaning 'no object' and is accepted; a path that fails to LOAD is refused, because keying null for a mistyped path is the same silent wrong answer.
set_spline_points: Author a spline's points - THIS IS WHAT MAKES NPCs WALK. The game routes wandering NPCs along BP_SegmentedPathTaskMarker, whose PathSpline is a USplineComponent. points is [{x,y,z},...] (min 2). point_type: curve|linear|constant|curveClamped|curveCustomTangent. snap_to_ground traces each point down onto the terrain, since a route authored at a flat Z floats or buries itself on uneven ground. Every point is validated BEFORE the existing spline is cleared: a component that is not a number fails the call naming points[N].<field>, rather than silently becoming 0 and bending the route through the origin. skip_post_edit_change=True is REQUIRED on any blueprint whose construction script rebuilds its own spline - BP_CarRoadSpline, BP_SplineSidewalk, BP_QuestNPCWalkPath and BP_SegmentedPathTaskMarker all do. Without it PostEditChange re-runs the construction script, which THROWS AWAY the points just written: the call still returns ok with the right pointCount and a read-back returns 2.
set_struct_member:
Rename, retype or re-default an EXISTING member of a Blueprint struct, in place.

Without this the only correction is remove + re-add, which mints a new GUID, APPENDS the member at
the end, reorders the struct, breaks every Make/Break Struct pin, and drops that column from every
row of every dependent DataTable. Fixing a typo was genuinely expensive.

Address the member by name or by guid (list_struct_members shows both). Pass at least one of
new_name, type or default.

Only works on Blueprint structs. A COOKED struct - which is every base-game DDS2 struct - is
refused, and that refusal is a safety feature: the engine's struct editing API asserts on a cooked
struct's stripped editor data rather than returning an error.

RETYPING IS DESTRUCTIVE DOWNSTREAM. The response reports dependentDataTables and warns when a
retype has reset that column in every row of every table built on the struct.
set_sublevel_streaming: Change a sublevel's streaming class: alwaysloaded | dynamic. DEFERRED (opId, poll list_sublevels) because SetStreamingClassForLevel does not edit a property - it REMOVES the ULevelStreaming and re-adds the level, returning a NEW object, and an object-identity swap mid-array is not an undoable property revert. Refuses when the sublevel is not loaded: the engine asserts (check(Level)) and takes the editor down rather than returning an error - load it with set_sublevel_visibility {should_be_loaded: True} first. Returns fromClass/toClass, and changed:false with no engine call when it is already that class.
set_sublevel_visibility: Flip a sublevel's flags: visible (EDITOR viewport visibility), should_be_loaded / should_be_visible (RUNTIME streaming intent), lighting_scenario. PARTIAL UPDATE - omitted flags are left alone, and a call that passes none of them is an error. EVERY write is READ BACK and compared: setters that do nothing are reported in ignored[{field, requested, actual, reason}] rather than echoed as success, and a call where NOTHING took is an ERROR. That is not belt-and-braces - ULevelStreamingAlwaysLoaded::ShouldBeLoaded() is hardcoded to return true, so should_be_loaded=False on an always-loaded sublevel (which is what add_sublevel creates by default) does nothing at all. Inline, not deferred, but the load/unload itself lands over later frames: check pending, then poll list_sublevels.
set_texture_settings: Set a Texture2D's CompressionSettings / SRGB / LODGroup / NeverStream / MipGenSettings / Filter. Enum values accept the short form or the engine spelling ('UserInterface2D' or 'TC_UserInterface2D'; 'UI' or 'TEXTUREGROUP_UI'; 'NoMipmaps' or 'TMGS_NoMipmaps'; 'Nearest' or 'TF_Nearest'); an unknown value errors with the accepted list and the nearest matches. For UI/shop icons: lod_group='UI', compression_settings='UserInterface2D', mip_gen_settings='NoMipmaps', never_stream=True - world-texture defaults give icons DXT banding, unused mips and streaming pop, which reads as a failed import. Every requested field is read back after the rebuild and any value the engine overruled is an ERROR naming requested-vs-applied, never a silent success. Refuses on a texture with no source data (a stub), because settings cannot make an empty texture render - import_texture with overwrite:true is what that needs.
set_variable_default: Set a member variable's default value (applied on next compile). value is REQUIRED and may be a string (UE export text) or typed JSON - a list for an array variable, an object for a struct, a number/bool for the matching type; it is converted against the variable's real property type and REFUSED if it cannot convert (an int variable rejects "banana" instead of storing it). Pass value=None to clear the default deliberately. Omitting value used to WIPE the existing default and report ok:true - that is now an error. Returns valueBefore/valueAfter/changed/typeValidated, all read back from the variable rather than echoed from the request.
set_variable_flags: Set Details-panel flags on a MEMBER variable (locals are rejected - they are never replicated or saved). PARTIAL UPDATE: omitted flags are left alone. rep_notify creates the OnRep_<Name> function graph if missing and implies replicated. replication_condition takes an ELifetimeCondition (COND_None, COND_OwnerOnly, ...; the COND_ prefix is optional). field_notify is the MVVM binding system's 'broadcasts on change' flag (the same checkbox the Blueprint Variables panel shows) - only meaningful on a class implementing INotifyFieldValueChanged, such as an MVVM ViewModel Blueprint (parent UMVVMViewModelBase). Returns the resulting flags, plus replicationWarning if the owning Actor has bReplicates=false.
set_variable_type: Retype an EXISTING variable's DECLARATION (every get/set node of it reconstructs to the new pin type). Same type grammar as add_variable: container = array|set|map, and for a map `type` is the KEY type with value_type the VALUE type. REFERENCE TYPES: the class goes INSIDE the type string - type='object:BP_Foo_C', not a separate class parameter. Prefixes: object:X (instance ref), class:X and subclassof:X (class ref / TSubclassOf), softobject:X and softclass:X (soft pointers). scope = member|local (local needs function). This changes the VARIABLE; to repoint a single NODE at a different declaring class use retarget_variable_node instead.
set_viewport_camera: Move the editor viewport camera the user is looking through. Distinct from capture_camera, which spawns a transient scene-capture and changes nothing on screen. look_at wins over rotation. ortho: top|bottom|front|back|left|right|perspective - orthographic top is the honest answer to 'show me the whole map', with no perspective falloff or far-clip surprises. rotation is x/y/z = pitch/yaw/roll like every other MifBridge transform. NOW ALSO SETS THE RENDERING STATE. view_mode takes a name (Lit, Unlit, Wireframe, LightingOnly, ShaderComplexity, DetailLighting, LightmapDensity, ReflectionOverride...) - the three that answer 'why is it black' fastest are Wireframe (is the mesh even there), Unlit (is the material broken) and LightingOnly (is anything lit). show_flags is a map like {'Fog': false, 'Bounds': true}; get_viewport_camera with show_flags='all' lists every valid name. AN UNKNOWN FLAG IS REFUSED, and that refusal prevents a CRASH rather than an error: FEngineShowFlags::SetSingleFlag ends its default branch in checkNoEntry(), so an unrecognised name would assert and take the editor down. Every name is validated before ANY is applied, so a typo in the fifth flag cannot leave the first four set. You can pass view_mode and show_flags together - the mode is applied first and the flags after, because SetViewMode internally rewrites show flags and doing it the other way round would silently discard yours. game_view hides editor-only sprites and grids.
set_water_body_spline: Replace a water body's spline - the spline IS the shape of a river or lake. points is an array of {x,y,z} in WORLD space and REPLACES the existing spline entirely; there is no append and no single-point setter, because ResetSpline is the only engine entry point that rebuilds the body's derived data and poking the spline component directly leaves those caches stale (a river the wrong shape, with no error anywhere). Resolves by actor PATH, not label. Needs at least 2 points. The response reads the spline back rather than echoing the request, and reports splineNote if the engine collapsed coincident points so the count differs from what you sent.
set_widget_animation_keys:
Key one channel of a widget's animation track.

property picks WHICH track to key and must match one you created with
add_widget_animation_track: RenderTransform.Translation, .Scale or .Shear (channel X or Y),
RenderTransform.Angle (leave channel empty - one curve), ColorAndOpacity (channel R, G, B or A),
or RenderOpacity (leave channel empty).

PROPERTY IS WHAT DISAMBIGUATES THE CHANNEL, and this matters. Translation, Angle, Scale and
Shear are all channels of the SAME section, so "X" alone is ambiguous - Scale.X and
Translation.X are different curves. Pass the property you actually mean; a channel that does not
belong to it is refused rather than falling through to a default curve.

keys is [{"time": seconds, "value": number, "interp": "cubic"|"linear"|"constant"}]. Times are
SECONDS and are converted to the MovieScene's tick space for you; the response reports each key
in both units so a bad conversion is visible. "cubic" uses the engine's Auto tangent, which is
what the UMG designer produces.

The whole batch is validated before anything is written, so a bad key cannot leave a half-keyed
curve. replace=True (the default) clears the channel first; pass False to append.

If the section's transform MASK has your channel switched off, it is turned on and the response
says maskWidened:true. The engine only evaluates a channel whose mask bit is set, so keys on a
masked-off channel would be stored and would animate nothing.
set_widget_animation_range:
Change an existing UMG animation's playback range or frame rate IN PLACE.

Exists so that correcting an animation's length no longer needs remove-and-recreate. That
sequence used to be the only way, and it crashed the editor: removing an animation left the
UObject alive holding its name, so recreating it renamed on top of a live object. Both halves of
that are fixed too, but not needing the dance at all is better.

Times are in SECONDS; give either or both bounds. displayRate is the editor's frame grid.

NO KEY MOVES. Key times live in the MovieScene's tick resolution, which is independent of
displayRate, so a longer range does not stretch the motion and a different frame rate does not
shift a single key. The response says keysUnchanged for exactly this reason - re-key with
set_widget_animation_keys if you wanted the motion rescaled.

Reports previousStartTime/previousEndTime alongside the new values, and reads the range back off
the MovieScene rather than echoing what you asked for.
shader_compile_status: Poll the editor-wide shader compiler (GShaderCompilingManager): {compiling, numRemainingJobs, numOutstandingJobs, numPendingJobs}. THE poll half for recompile_material / create_material (and level-load shader churn). Numbers decrease toward zero; compiling=false with numRemainingJobs=0 means quiescent - safe to read material statistics or capture pixels.
snap_actors_to_ground: Drop actors onto the terrain, one trace each, with the actor ITSELF excluded from the trace. Doing this from outside is both slow (one HTTP round-trip per actor) and wrong - a trace at a building's own XY hits its roof and 'snaps' it onto itself, climbing every call. Places the BOTTOM of each actor's bounds on the hit, so pivots that are not at the base still sit correctly. Landscapes are skipped. Requires a selector (actor_paths / folder / label_contains / all) - it refuses to guess. By DEFAULT only a Landscape counts as ground, so furniture dropped onto a floor, table or counter finds nothing: pass ground_actor='<label, name or path of the surface>' to nominate that actor as the ground, or allow_any_hit=True to accept the first thing hit.
source_control:
Report whether revision control is configured, and what state a file is in (checked out, checked out by someone else, added, not at head, read-only on disk). Omit path for the provider status alone. READ ONLY - source_control_checkout is the write half.

NOT BEING UNDER REVISION CONTROL IS A NORMAL ANSWER, not a failure: enabled:false comes back with ok:true and a plain statement that no checkout is needed. That is what a solo project looks like. With no provider it still reports readOnlyOnDisk when it can, because that is the one thing left that would stop a save.

IT DOES NOT QUERY AN UNREACHABLE SERVER. QueryFileState is not a local read - the engine builds an FUpdateStatus with SetUpdateModifiedState(true) and runs Provider->Execute SYNCHRONOUSLY, and MifBridge dispatches on the game thread, so asking a configured-but-unavailable provider would freeze the editor until it timed out. IsAvailable() is checked first and the response says when the query was skipped for that reason.

One path at a time, deliberately: a plural form would be a loop of blocking server calls, and the engine's plural QueryFileStates does not exist before 5.6 anyway.
source_control_checkout:
Check out, mark for add, or REVERT a file in revision control. action is checkout, add, checkoutOrAdd or revert; revert requires confirm=True because it discards local changes. Checking IN is deliberately not offered.

SEPARATE FROM source_control ON PURPOSE. The safety gate classifies whole endpoints, not actions - so a single endpoint carrying both would either let revert discard work in read mode, or make a harmless status query unavailable in scratch mode. Split, the read is always allowed and this half sits on the gate with every other persist-to-disk verb, which means it is refused outside `full` write mode.

CHECKING IN IS NOT OFFERED and will not be: a submit publishes work to everyone on the team, which is a person's decision rather than an agent's.

The result is READ BACK - these helpers return a bool and nothing about the resulting state, so isCheckedOut and readOnlyOnDisk in the response are queried afterwards rather than assumed from success.
spawn_actor_in_level: Spawn an actor into the current level. actor_class may be a native class or a Blueprint class path (/Game/BP/BP_Foo.BP_Foo_C). location/rotation/scale take {x,y,z} (rotation also accepts {pitch,yaw,roll}, and scale accepts a bare number for uniform); rotation is pitch/yaw/roll. mesh assigns a static mesh (spawn a StaticMeshActor for it) - it used to be accepted and silently dropped, producing an EMPTY actor that reported ok. Transforms are validated BEFORE the spawn, so a bad component fails without leaving an actor behind. EVERY numeric field is strict now: a value you SUPPLY that is not a number is a hard error naming the field, the value and the expected type. It is never defaulted - location={"x":"not-a-number","y":123,"z":456} used to return ok:true having applied y and z, kept the old x, and echoed the mixture back as if you had asked for it. Returns the new actorPath. The level is left DIRTY - call save_package on the map path to persist.
spawn_actor_in_pie: Spawn an actor into the RUNNING PIE world. spawn_actor_in_level cannot do this - it goes through UEditorActorSubsystem, which serves the EDITOR world. Needed because a mod whose bootstrap is UE4SS (which does not run in the editor) otherwise never spawns under PIE, and placing the actor in the map does not survive a world travel. net_mode picks which PIE world when running multi-client: server (default - a replicated actor spawned here reaches every client), client, or any. Returns hasAuthority/replicates on the spawned actor plus a worlds array of every PIE world, so a wrong-role spawn is visible rather than silent. BeginPlay fires immediately; the actor is not saved to any map and dies with PIE. rotation is x/y/z = pitch/yaw/roll like every other MifBridge transform. mesh assigns a static mesh (spawn a StaticMeshActor for it) - the same parameter spawn_actor_in_level takes, ported here because this endpoint was the unfixed sibling that still accepted it and silently dropped it, producing an EMPTY actor that reported ok.
spawn_many: Spawn MANY actors in ONE call. items is a list of {x,y,z or location:{}, rotation:{} or yaw, scale (number or {}), label?, mesh?, material?}. Top-level mesh/material are the defaults; per-item values override. label_prefix names them '<prefix>_<index>' - without it every actor is 'StaticMeshActor_417', unfindable by label and invisible to anything that filters on one (snap_actors_to_ground's label_contains). Replaces the 2-HTTP-calls-per-actor pattern - a few hundred actors goes from minutes to seconds. Capped at 5000 per call; returns spawned/failed counts. A transform component that is not a number now fails THAT item with a reason naming items[N].<field> and counts it in failed[], instead of defaulting to 0 and placing the actor at an address you did not give. Unrecognised keys inside an entry are still ignored - only the transform values are checked.
spawn_metahuman_actor: Spawn a live preview actor in the open level bound to the UMetaHumanCharacter asset at `character_path`. Calls TryAddObjectToEdit then SpawnMetaHumanActor - the same two calls the MetaHuman Character editor makes on open - and leaves the character registered for editing afterward (editingSessionOpen:true in the response) so the actor keeps reflecting changes; there is no remove-from-edit endpoint yet. UE 5.6+ only. Not saved: the actor is a normal placed actor in the open level.
start_pie: Start Play-In-Editor. DOES NOT BLOCK: the engine defers the start to its next tick, and this handler runs on the game thread, so waiting here would deadlock the very ticks PIE needs. Poll pie_status until state=='running' before asserting on runtime state. simulate=True runs the world WITHOUT possessing a pawn - better for observing systems tick, since it needs no PlayerStart and cannot fail on a missing GameMode. For replication work: players (1-8) and net_mode (standalone|listen|client, defaulting to listen when players>1) launch a real multiplayer session, one_process (default True) keeps the clients in this process, and width/height size the client windows. Testing anything RepNotify / RunOnServer / NetMulticast needs players>1 - a standalone PIE always has authority and will make authority-gated code look like it works.
thumbnail_capabilities: Preflight for the thumbnail endpoints. With no argument: whether this editor can render at all (canRender, canEverRender, rhiInitialized, thumbnailManager) plus size limits. With an asset path: its class, the UThumbnailRenderer the engine would use (renderer/hasRenderer), whether it already has a custom cached thumbnail, and whether it supports orbit camera control. hasRenderer:false means the Content Browser only shows it a generic class icon and render_thumbnail / write_thumbnail_texture will REFUSE rather than bake a black square - ask here first instead of debugging a failed bake. Also reports whether the ThumbnailGenerator plugin is loaded; MifBridge deliberately does not use it.
trace:
Trace a ray or sweep a shape through the world.

trace_ground only fires straight down and takes the first GROUND hit. This answers everything
else: is there a wall between these two points, what is along this direction, does this doorway
fit a capsule of this size.

Give start plus either end, or direction + distance. shape may be line (default), sphere, box or
capsule - the non-line shapes SWEEP, which is how you ask whether something fits. channel is one
of worldStatic, worldDynamic, visibility, camera, pawn, physicsBody.

ignore_actors names actors to exclude. An entry that does not resolve is REFUSED rather than
skipped, because a trace that silently ignores nothing can return a confident hit against the
very actor you excluded.

draw=True leaves the ray in the viewport for draw_duration seconds. The response reports which
world was traced and whether PIE is running.
trace_ground:
Line-trace straight down to find ground height.

Pass either x/y or location={"x":..,"y":..,"z":..} (its z seeds from_z). The response echoes the
coordinates actually traced - check them. Passing a location the endpoint ignored is how an
entire terrain investigation once got run at the world origin and concluded the ground was flat
everywhere.

Returns hit=false honestly when nothing is hit: editor-world collision is NOT guaranteed for
imported meshes, and treating a miss as z=0 is how things end up floating.
trace_start: Start an Unreal Insights trace, writing a .utrace under Saved/MifBridge/Traces. This is the answer to 'which Blueprint is burning frame time' that perf_heavy_actors cannot give: that one reports a static CENSUS (triangles, components, which actors tick), while a trace shows each Tick by name with its real cost. Default channels cpu,frame,bookmark,stats. Tracing costs performance while it runs - do the thing you want to measure, then call trace_stop.
trace_stop: Stop the trace started by trace_start and report where the file went and how big it is. The size is the evidence it captured anything - a zero-byte trace means the channels produced no data, which otherwise looks identical to success. Stopping when nothing was started is not an error; it answers stopped:false so the call stays idempotent.
ui_scenario_activate: THE hazardous step of the scenario runner: delivers activation_key through UGameViewportClient::InputKey - the actual entry point real input takes into the game's own PlayerController/input stack, not a generic focused-widget guess. This runs mod gameplay code (OnClicked, Construct, Tick, whatever responds) SYNCHRONOUSLY on the handler thread; requires confirm=True. After this call, poll ui_scenario_status until state is READY, TIMED_OUT, or FAILED - READY means expected_widget_classes (if given) are all present and the live widget count has held steady for stable_frames consecutive ticks. The timeout_seconds deadline is real but can only catch 'the condition never became true' - if the game thread itself hangs (an infinite loop in mod code), no timeout on that same thread can interrupt it; that's the existing modal-hang situation, not something new here. Call ui_scenario_start first.
ui_scenario_capture: Capture the scenario's result: the GAME viewport (not the editor's own active viewport - a different capture entirely from capture_viewport) as a PNG, plus every top-level live widget's path/class/geometry. Only valid once ui_scenario_status reports state READY. Pass any reported path to describe_live_widget for its full nested tree. fidelity in the response is 'pieActualInput' - PIE evidence, not packaged-runtime evidence (MifBridge is Editor-only).
ui_scenario_start: Start an interaction-faithful UI scenario: positions the LOCAL PLAYER PAWN at player_location/player_rotation (explicit - no automatic interaction-radius calculation, since that's game-specific logic this bridge can't know generically) in a running PIE world (net_mode: server|client|any). Requires confirm=True - it's a real gameplay-state mutation. Only ONE scenario runs at a time; call ui_scenario_stop before starting another. This does NOT manage PIE lifecycle - start_pie/pie_status first. Follow with ui_scenario_activate to actually press the key.
ui_scenario_status: Poll the active UI scenario's state: IDLE (none active) | POSITIONED (after ui_scenario_start) | WAITING_FOR_STABLE_UI (after ui_scenario_activate, still ticking) | READY (capture-able) | TIMED_OUT | FAILED | STOPPED. Also reports elapsedSeconds, lastWidgetCount, stableFramesObserved/Required, and whether the world/pawn/target are still valid.
ui_scenario_stop: Stop the active UI scenario (if any) and return this bridge to idle - unregisters the internal ticker and clears state. Safe to call even if nothing is active (wasActive:false). Does not restore the player pawn's original position or undo anything the activation's gameplay code did; call this when done with a scenario regardless of how it ended.
undo_transactions: Undo the last N editor transactions (count 1..50), or pass to_index to undo down until currentIndex == to_index (-1 = undo everything; capped at 50 steps per call - call again to continue). count and to_index are mutually exclusive. Returns undone, titlesUndone, stoppedEarly(+reason), and the new queueLength/undoCount/currentIndex. WARNING: undoing a Blueprint-touching transaction reinstances classes - RE-RESOLVE any cached object paths afterwards. allow_redo=False makes the undone steps unredoable.
unmap_input_key: Remove key bindings from an InputMappingContext. With action and key, unbinds that one pair; with action alone, unbinds EVERY key from that one action; with all=True AND confirm=True, clears the entire context. An omitted key never means 'delete everything' - clearing has to be asked for by name and confirmed, because it cannot be undone through this endpoint. `removed` is the measured change in the mapping count, not the request: UnmapKey and UnmapAllKeysFromAction both return void and report nothing about whether they matched, so unmapping something that was not bound succeeds with removed:0. The context is left dirty and NOT saved.
unmap_legacy_input: Remove a LEGACY input binding from UInputSettings. A legacy mapping matches on name, key AND every modifier, so removing Ctrl+S needs ctrl=True - without it you are asking to remove a different binding and nothing will match. `removed` is the measured change in the mapping count, not the request: RemoveActionMapping and RemoveAxisMapping both return void and report nothing about whether they matched, so an unmatched removal succeeds with removed:0 and a note explaining why. In-memory only, like map_legacy_input.
wrap_tree_widget: The Designer's 'Wrap With': insert a new panel where the widget currently sits, then move the widget inside it. wrapper_class must be a UPanelWidget (CanvasPanel, VerticalBox, HorizontalBox, Overlay, SizeBox, Border...). Sibling order is preserved - the wrapper takes the original's exact child index. Handles the ROOT case, which has no parent slot to inherit. Compile to apply.
write_datatable_rows: Write DataTable rows (each a dict with a 'Name' field + row-struct fields). replace=True overwrites the whole table; otherwise rows are added/updated in place. Requires confirm=True. FText asymmetry: merge mode (replace=False, the default) parses values through FJsonObjectConverter and accepts read_datatable's NSLOCTEXT export form verbatim; replace mode assigns a GENERATED localization id (namespace '<Table> [guid]', key '<Row>_<Column>') to any plain FText string, so those fields read back as NSLOCTEXT(...) - a successful replace on a row struct with FText returns textLocalizationNote saying so. Prefer merge unless you intend a full-table overwrite.
write_thumbnail_texture: Render an asset's icon and WRITE IT AS A UTexture2D ASSET at texture_path - the endpoint that actually fills an empty icon stub, because a PNG cannot be referenced by a widget. Two modes. CREATE: texture_path does not exist -> new package + UTexture2D (compression defaults to EditorIcon/UserInterface2D uncompressed RGBA, lod_group UI, no mips - the right settings for a UI icon). REFILL: texture_path already exists and overwrite:true -> the EXISTING UTexture2D's source is replaced in place, so its object path and every widget/data-table/material already pointing at it keep working; settings you do NOT pass are left exactly as the stub's author set them. Refuses (without writing anything) if the destination exists and overwrite is false, if it is not a UTexture2D, or if it lives in a cooked package (FTextureSource is stripped at cook). The SOURCE asset may be cooked - cooked meshes render fine. save defaults true and the response is only ok after Source.IsValid(), the source dimensions, the object path and the .uasset on disk have all been re-read. SelfManaged, so `batch` refuses it: N icons is N calls, each fully verified. compression: EditorIcon | UserInterface2D | Default | VectorDisplacementmap | Grayscale. lod_group: UI | World | Character | none.
blueprint_watch:
Watch a Blueprint pin and read its live value without editing the asset. op: add | remove | list | clear | read.

CLEAR IS NOT REMOVE, and this is the trap worth knowing before you use it. `clear` is BLUEPRINT-WIDE: it removes EVERY watch on the blueprint, not the one you name. Passing node_guid or pin alongside op:clear used to be accepted and silently dropped, so a call that read as 'clear this one watch' deleted all of them and answered removed:7 - which looks like confirmation. It is refused now, and the refusal names op:remove, which is the verb that was meant. Use op:remove with node_guid and pin to remove ONE.

Watches are EDITOR-ONLY state on the loaded UBlueprint. They are not saved with the asset and are gone after a restart, so there is nothing to undo a wrong clear with.

A read with no value still SUCCEEDS and says which nothing it is: noDebugObject (no PIE session or no instance selected), notInScope (running, but not at a point where the pin holds anything), or noProperty (the pin has no backing property, so no session will ever produce one). Reading a VALUE needs a live PIE session.
blueprint_breakpoint:
Set, clear and list Blueprint breakpoints without editing the asset. op: add | remove | enable | disable | list | clear.

CLEAR IS NOT REMOVE - the same trap as blueprint_watch. `clear` removes EVERY breakpoint on the blueprint; passing node_guid with it used to be silently dropped, so a call meaning 'clear the breakpoint on this node' deleted all of them. It is refused now and names op:remove instead. Breakpoints are editor-only state, not saved with the asset, so nothing undoes it.

enable/disable REFUSE when there is no breakpoint rather than creating one, so a typo'd guid cannot leave a breakpoint somewhere you never looked. This replaces the splice-a-print-node workaround, which mutates somebody's blueprint four times to answer a read-only question.
delete_asset:
Delete a /Game/ asset package. Requires confirm=True.

WHEN IT REFUSES IT TELLS YOU WHO IS HOLDING IT, and reading that is the difference between one call and an hour. `blockedBy` carries five separate answers, not one flag:
  openAssetEditors     - N asset editors still have it open. Call close_asset_editors first.
  registryReferencers  - N packages reference it ON DISK.
  rootedInMemory       - the object is ROOTED, so garbage collection will not release it.
  memoryReferencers    - N live objects in memory still point at it.
  transactionBuffer    - the editor's UNDO HISTORY is holding it. That history belongs to the person at the keyboard, so this endpoint will NOT clear it; an editor restart releases it.

READ memoryReferencers, NOT registryReferencers, for anything you just made. The registry records references saved to DISK and is EMPTY for an unsaved asset however many live objects point at it - the handler says so in its own registryNote. An unsaved scratch asset that refuses to delete will show registryReferencers:[] and a populated memoryReferencers.

DELETING IS NOT THE SAME AS GONE. It unregisters the asset while the UObject stays resident, and the registry can re-discover it later (docs/06 #28) - so a find_assets after a successful delete can still list it. Judge by what you asked for, not by a later folder scan.

Ordering matters when deleting several: a mesh REFERENCES its skeleton, so deleting the skeleton first is refused, correctly. Walk dependents before dependencies.
delete_level_actor:
Delete a placed actor from the current level. Requires confirm=True.

THIS WRITES TO WHATEVER LEVEL IS OPEN, which is the level the person at the keyboard is looking at. Addressed by actorPath - list_level_actors reports it.

Actors spawned by endpoints like add_nav_volume, create_water_body and create_landscape go into the EDITOR world rather than a PIE-scoped one, so stopping PIE does NOT remove them - they persist in the level and accumulate one per run. Anything you spawn, delete. (mifaudit.cleanup_level_actor exists for exactly this and says the same.)
fix_up_redirectors:
Sweep a /Game folder and resolve its redirectors. Requires confirm=True.

USE dryRun:True FIRST. It needs NO confirm and changes nothing, and it tells you what the real run would do. This is the widest-blast-radius endpoint in the bridge: it DELETES redirector packages and REWRITES every referencer that points at them, across whatever folder you named.

Only one fixup can run in an editor at a time - a second call is refused with 'a redirector fixup is already running', and NOTHING is started, so the refusal is safe to retry later.

`path` is required and is the folder to sweep (e.g. /Game/Mods/MyMod). Sweeping /Game entire is legal and rarely what you want.
remove_variable:
Delete a Blueprint variable. blueprintId (alias: path), name, confirm=True.

AN INHERITED VARIABLE CANNOT BE REMOVED HERE and the refusal names which parent declares it - a blueprint cannot remove what it does not own. Change it on the parent, or override the value rather than the declaration.
remove_function:
Delete a Blueprint function graph. blueprintId (alias: path), name, confirm=True.

THE KEY IS `name`, not `function`. `function` belongs to implement_interface_function, and the endpoint says so rather than failing vaguely - a wrong key here would otherwise read as 'no such function'.
remove_interface:
Remove an implemented interface from a Blueprint. blueprintId (alias: path), interface (aliases: interfaceClass, class), confirm=True.

IT ALWAYS TAKES THE FUNCTIONS WITH IT. There is no preserve option - the engine call runs with bPreserveFunctions=false, so every function the interface contributed goes too. If you want the bodies kept, copy them out first; nothing here will do it for you.
revert_inherited_component:
Discard a component's per-child overrides. blueprint (aliases: blueprintId, path, asset), component (aliases: componentName, name), confirm=True.

IT DISCARDS EVERY OVERRIDDEN PROPERTY ON THAT COMPONENT IN ONE STEP - not the one you were thinking of. There is no per-property revert. Read the overrides first if you need any of them.

This is the undo for override_inherited_component, which is why THAT endpoint treats confirm as optional: minting an override is reversible, discarding one is not.
rename_variable:
Rename a Blueprint variable. blueprintId (alias: path), oldName, newName, confirm=True.

BOTH oldName AND newName are required - there is no single `name` key, and passing one is refused rather than guessed at.
rename_event_dispatcher:
Rename an event dispatcher. blueprintId (alias: path), oldName (aliases: name, dispatcher), newName (alias: to), confirm=True.

THE ALIASES ARE ASYMMETRIC and that is deliberate: the CURRENT name accepts name/dispatcher, and only the DESTINATION has the short spelling `to`. So `name` means the old one. Passing `name` expecting it to mean the new one renames nothing and is the mistake worth naming.
remove_tree_widget:
Remove a widget from a Widget Blueprint's tree. blueprintId (alias: path), widgetName, confirm=True.

IT REMOVES THE WHOLE SUBTREE in one call - every child of the named widget goes with it. That is why it is confirm-gated. list_tree_widgets first if you are not certain what hangs below it.
remove_anim_curve:
Remove a curve from an animation. assetPath (aliases: path, animation), name, type (float|transform, default float), confirm=True.

THE CURVE'S KEYS GO WITH IT - the endpoint says so in its own accepted summary. This is not a mute or a disable.

`type` is part of the address, not a hint: float and transform are separate curve sets, so the name alone does not identify a curve.
pcg_cleanup:
Clear what a PCG component generated. actorPath (an actor with a PCG component), confirm=True.

IT DESTROYS THE ACTORS THE PCG COMPONENT SPAWNED - the endpoint's own refusal says so, which is why it is confirm-gated. It is addressed by the ACTOR that owns the component, not by the graph.
remove_struct_member:
Remove a member from a User Defined Struct. struct (aliases: structPath, path), name OR guid, confirm=True.

ADDRESSED BY NAME OR GUID, NEVER BY INDEX - `index` is remove_enum_value's parameter and is refused here by name rather than silently misread. Members are GUID-keyed internally and a name is resolved to one, so the guid is the unambiguous form.

A struct is a TYPE: anything built on it - DataTables using it as a row type, split-struct pins - is affected by removing a field. Check what depends on the struct before removing, because this endpoint reports on the struct and not on its consumers.
rename_asset:
Rename or move a /Game/ asset package, leaving a redirector. Requires confirm=True.

PASS renames=[{path, newPath}, ...] FOR SEVERAL AT ONCE, and that is not the same as looping. One IAssetTools pass fixes references BETWEEN the renamed assets together; renaming them one at a time leaves each earlier rename pointing through a redirector at the next.

A REDIRECTOR IS LEFT BEHIND on purpose - that is what keeps existing references working. It is not litter to be cleaned up blindly: fix_up_redirectors DELETES them and rewrites every referencer, so run that with dryRun:true first and only against the folder you mean.
bl_set_light:
Change a light that already exists. Before this op a light could be created and never adjusted: there was no set path and no read path, and bl_object_info returns early for a light and reports only its transform.

WHICH LIGHT. `object` is required and names the light OBJECT, not the light datablock. A name that is not a LIGHT is refused by type, and a name that does not exist is refused with the lights that DO exist listed.

RETYPING. Passing `type` changes the light's kind (POINT/SUN/SPOT/AREA), and per-type settings in the same call are judged against the type the light will BE afterwards - so {type:'SPOT', spot_angle:0.5} is legal, while spot_angle on a light being retyped to POINT is refused. Blender DISCARDS a per-type property when you leave that type; changedFields is where that shows up.

PER-TYPE KEYS, refused on the wrong type rather than ignored: spot_angle/spot_blend are SPOT only, size/size_y/shape are AREA only, angle is SUN only, radius (the soft-shadow size) is POINT or SPOT. The same table guards bl_create_light.

REFUSALS FIRE BEFORE ANY WRITE. A call naming one bad key leaves the light in exactly the state it was in.

THE RESPONSE carries `before`, `after`, `changedFields` and `changedAnything`, all read off the datablock after view_layer.update(). Setting a value to what it already was reports changedAnything false, which is the honest answer rather than an assumed success.

RADIANS for rotation, spot_angle and angle, like every other op here.
bl_list_lights:
Every light in the file with its full state. The read path that did not exist: bl_object_info returns early for a light and gives only the transform, so nothing could report a light's energy, colour, cone or shadow.

FILTERS. `name_contains` is a case-insensitive substring; `type` is POINT/SUN/SPOT/AREA and is validated against this Blender's own enum, so an unknown type is refused rather than silently matching nothing.

PER-LIGHT FIELDS are the same shape bl_create_light and bl_set_light return, from one shared reader, so the three cannot drift apart: type, energy, color, location, rotationEuler, diffuseFactor, specularFactor, plus the per-type ones (shadowSoftSize for POINT/SPOT, spotSize/spotBlend for SPOT, size/sizeY/shape for AREA, angle for SUN) and `shadow` when this Blender still carries use_shadow on the light.

hideViewport and hideRender are included because a correctly configured light that is hidden from the render reads as perfect in every other field, and that is the usual reason a scene comes back black. `sceneHasAnyLight` answers that question directly.

WHAT IS NOT LISTED: a light DATABLOCK with no object. It cannot illuminate anything until something links it, and bl_clear_scene purges those.
bl_save_file:
Write the Blender session to a .blend. Until 2026-09-03 the addon had no save path at all, so every light, camera, world, keyframe, physics setup and node group it authored died with the process - the only artefacts it could produce were a mesh FBX, a baked texture and one rendered frame.

SAVE-A-COPY IS THE DEFAULT. Blender's own save-as normally REPOINTS the session at the new path, so a later save silently goes somewhere the caller never named. This passes copy=True unless repoint_session is set, leaving bpy.data.filepath alone; the response reports sessionFilepathUnchanged so you can see which happened.

OVERWRITE IS REFUSED BY DEFAULT. An existing file needs overwrite:true. Every refusal fires before anything is written, so a rejected call leaves the disk untouched. Missing parent directories are created.

THE FIELD TO READ IS purgedOrphans. Blender DELETES datablocks with no users and no fake user when it writes - an action unlinked from its object, an image nothing points at, a node group nobody instanced. That is permanent, silent, and caused BY the successful save. They are counted BEFORE the write, because afterwards they do not exist to count, and reported by type and name. Give one a fake user first if you want to keep it.

Success is stat'd off disk - a save that raises no error but leaves no file, or an empty one, is reported as a failure.
bl_open_file:
Open a .blend, discarding everything currently in memory. This is the one Blender op here that can lose work which was never on disk.

AN OPEN OVER A DIRTY SESSION IS REFUSED unless discard_unsaved:true. There is no undo across a file load, so the guard is not optional - save first with bl_save_file if the work matters. A missing file is refused before anything is touched.

AFTERWARDS IT RE-READS bpy.data.filepath and refuses to report success if the session did not actually become the file you asked for, rather than trusting that a silent load means it worked. The response carries the datablock counts so a caller can tell immediately whether the file is what they expected.
bl_file_info:
What .blend this session is, whether it has unsaved work, and what it holds. No parameters, cheap enough to call first.

It answers the two questions that decide whether a session can be resumed at all: is there a file on disk behind this (isSaved, fileExists, fileBytes), and is there work in memory that is not in it (isDirty).

orphanCount and orphans are the reason to call it before saving. They list datablocks with no users and no fake user, across actions, images, materials, meshes, node groups, textures, armatures, cameras, lights, worlds, curves, collections and objects. A SAVE DELETES ALL OF THEM, permanently and without a word. Seeing the list first is the only warning you get.

counts is a per-type census of the file, which is the cheapest way for a caller to orient itself in a scene it did not build.
bl_render_info:
Everything that decides what a render will look like, and why it will be black. The read half of bl_set_render_settings, which reports only the five fields it can write - ops_render had no read op at all, one of six modules in that state.

THE BLACK-RENDER QUESTION IS ANSWERED DIRECTLY. The 'blockers' field lists measured reasons the render will produce nothing useful, in the order they bite: no scene camera (nothing else will tell you - scene_info omits it); no world datablock, which means the scene contributes NO ambient light, so anything not lit by its own fixture is pure black and the lights get blamed; every light hidden from render or at zero energy; and a zero effective resolution. 'wouldRenderSomething' is the one-field version of the same answer.

SAMPLES ARE REPORTED WITH THE PROPERTY THEY LIVE ON. The count sits on cycles.samples or on eevee.taa_render_samples depending on the engine, and a caller comparing it against what they set needs to know it is the same field. 'samplesOn' names it.

'effectiveResolution' is the resolution multiplied by the percentage, which is the size the file will actually be and the number people get wrong, because percentage is a multiplier nobody remembers is set.

COLOUR MANAGEMENT is included - view transform, look, exposure, gamma, display device - because it silently changes every pixel and is the usual cause of 'washed out'. The default view transform differs by Blender version and a studio OCIO config renames all of them, so these are read off the scene rather than assumed.
bl_set_camera:
Change a camera that already exists. Same absence bl_set_light closed for lights: a camera could be created and never adjusted.

SWITCHING THE SCENE CAMERA is the part that was genuinely unreachable. make_active existed only on bl_create_camera, so choosing between two cameras that already exist - ordinary shot work - meant bl_run_python or deleting and recreating one, which loses its name to Blender's .001 uniquify and drops any keyframes on the datablock.

sensor_fit is included because without it sensor_width is a half-answer. AUTO fits the focal length to the LARGER render dimension, so a portrait render silently changes which sensor dimension the lens is measured against, and no real-world lens can be matched without saying which.

TYPE-GATED SETTINGS are judged against the type the camera will BE after this call, so {type:'ORTHO', ortho_scale:5} works in one call while ortho_scale on a camera being retyped to PERSP is refused. Every refusal fires before any write.

look_at and rotation are refused together - two answers to the same question. The response carries before, after and changedFields, with fovDegrees derived at the current render resolution.
bl_list_cameras:
Every camera in the file, and which one the scene renders through.

sceneCamera was unobtainable anywhere in this addon. bl_scene_info does not report it, bl_set_render_settings gives only a boolean saying whether one exists, and bl_render_still names it only as a side effect of blocking for an entire render. It is the first thing anybody needs to know about a scene they did not build.

Each row carries the full optical set - lens, sensor width/height/fit, clipping, shift, ortho scale, depth of field including its focus OBJECT - plus fovRadians and fovDegrees derived at the current render resolution. FOV is the number that actually determines framing, it depends on sensor fit as well as focal length, and computing it wrong is the usual reason a camera looks right in the numbers and wrong in the render.

hideViewport and hideRender are reported for the same reason bl_list_lights reports them: a hidden object reads as perfectly configured in every other field.
bl_aim_object:
Point any object at another object or at a point, and measure that it now points there.

Nothing could aim anything after creation. bl_create_camera accepted look_at at birth and was the only user of the aiming maths; a light could not be aimed at all, which makes a spot light close to unusable through this bridge.

Pass exactly one of target (an object - its world-space origin is used) or look_at (a point). Both, or neither, is refused.

THE POSTCONDITION IS THE ANGLE, not the euler. It reports the angle between the object's world-space local -Z and the direction to the target, measured AFTER the write, and refuses above about 1e-3 radians. That is deliberate: the derivation this op depends on was once wrong by exactly pi, aiming a camera 166 degrees away from its target while returning a perfectly plausible euler. Reading back the rotation you just wrote cannot catch that, because it cannot disagree with itself.

Blender aims down LOCAL -Z for lights and cameras alike.
bl_list_animation_data:
Every route by which an object is animated. bl_list_keyframes walks animation_data.action, which is ONE OF THREE places animation lives - drivers are on animation_data.drivers and NLA strips on animation_data.nla_tracks, both separate collections. So an object driven entirely by drivers came back with curveCount 0 from an op whose entire purpose is verification. That is a WRONG answer, not a missing one, and a caller checking whether their driver landed was told it had not.

REPORTS: animatedBy (action / drivers / nla) and isAnimated; the action name and whether it has a fake user, because an action WITHOUT one is deleted on save and that is silent data loss; each drivers expression, type, validity and the objects its variables point at; and every NLA track with its strips and frame ranges.

invalidDrivers is the field to watch. A driver whose variable targets a deleted object stays in place, evaluates to zero, and reports nothing anywhere in Blenders UI or in any other op here.
bl_delete_keyframe:
Remove keyframes from a channel - the correction path bl_set_keyframe never had, which forced delete-and-recreate for any mistake.

Omit frame to clear EVERY key on the path; omit index to clear every array element. A path with no fcurve is refused with a pointer to bl_list_keyframes rather than reported as a successful deletion of nothing.

COUNTED OFF THE CURVES, before and after. Blenders keyframe removal reports a bool that is False both for there-was-nothing-there and for it-refused, and those are different answers. The response carries keyframesBefore, keyframesAfter, removed and countsAgree - the last is this op checking its own arithmetic against the curve instead of asking you to trust it.

Keys are removed in REVERSE order, because removing during an ascending walk shifts the collection underneath and silently skips every second key.
bl_set_object_visibility:
Control what an object is visible TO: the viewport, the render, and each ray type separately.

THE ONE PEOPLE WANT IS visible_glossy. Setting it false stops a softbox or a bounce card appearing as a white rectangle in every reflection, which is the single most common adjustment in product and archviz lighting, and nothing in this addon could reach it.

IT ALSO ANSWERS WHY AN OBJECT IS MISSING FROM A RENDER. hide_render and visible_camera are exactly where that lives, and the response reports appearsInRender directly rather than leaving you to combine them.

For EVERY object type, not lights alone: ray visibility is an OBJECT property, and a mesh acting as a reflector, a holdout or a shadow catcher needs it as much as a lamp does.

holdout cuts the object out of the render as alpha; indirect_only (shadow catcher) keeps its contribution to bounce light while removing it from camera.

VERSION HANDLING: ray visibility moved off the Cycles addon onto the object itself in Blender 3.0, so both spellings are tried, newest first. A flag this build does not expose is REFUSED BY NAME rather than silently ignored - the mistake the shadow key on bl_create_light made until it was fixed the same day - and every requested flag is resolved BEFORE any is written, so a build that lacks one refuses the whole call instead of applying half of them.
bl_evaluate_at_frame:
What an object ACTUALLY is at given frames, read through the evaluated depsgraph.

WHY IT EXISTS. Every other read in this addon reads the RAW property off the datablock, and that is not the value the scene evaluates to whenever a constraint, driver, NLA stack, parent or simulation cache is involved. A constraint does not touch obj.matrix_world AT ALL - so reading the base object reports every constraint as having done nothing, and reading back the value you just wrote is a proxy that cannot fail. Nothing procedural can be verified without this, which is why it is the first thing built in its tier rather than the most interesting.

PASS A LIST OF FRAMES. A single number is accepted and wrapped. data_paths adds extra properties sampled at each frame, resolved on the EVALUATED object; one that does not resolve reports its error in place rather than failing the whole call.

THE SCENE FRAME IS RESTORED, and the restoration is asserted rather than assumed. This op moves frame_current in order to sample, and leaving somebody on frame 47 as a side effect of a READ is the kind of quiet damage this bridge exists to refuse. frameRestored and startedOnFrame are both reported.

movedAcrossFrames answers the question behind most uses of this op. A list of identical matrices is exactly what a dead driver, a muted NLA track, a constraint pointing at a deleted target and a bake that lost its motion all look like.

The depsgraph is re-fetched every frame on purpose: the evaluated object is a temporary the depsgraph owns, and holding one across a frame change reads stale data that looks plausible.
bl_edit_fcurve:
Change how a curve moves BETWEEN its keys - interpolation, easing, handle type, extrapolation.

bl_set_keyframe can set an interpolation at INSERT time and reaches three of Blenders thirteen. Nothing could change one afterwards, and nothing could touch EASING at all - which is most of the craft in motion graphics, where BACK with ease-out against LINEAR is the entire look. Retiming or re-feeling an existing animation meant deleting and re-keying it.

easing is the DIRECTION an easing interpolation runs (AUTO / EASE_IN / EASE_OUT / EASE_IN_OUT) and is meaningless without one of the easing interpolations set.

extrapolation is a property of the CURVE, not of its keys, and controls what happens outside the keyed range - which is a different question from looping, and a much blunter answer than a CYCLES modifier.

Omit frame to apply to every key on the curve; omit index for every array element. Every enum is validated against this Blenders own RNA rather than a remembered list, and everything is checked before anything is written.
bl_add_fcurve_modifier:
Put a modifier on a curve. The one that matters is CYCLES, which is how an animation LOOPS.

There was no way to loop anything through this addon. Every turntable, idle, cycling fan and blinking light had to be keyed out to its full length by hand, and a two-key rotation could not be made to repeat at all. Blender has had this forever; the bridge simply never exposed it.

A CYCLES modifier on a curve with FEWER THAN TWO keyframes is refused. There is no cycle to repeat, and Blender will add the modifier anyway and do nothing with it - which looks exactly like success and is the failure this op exists to prevent.

modeBefore and modeAfter (NONE / REPEAT / REPEAT_OFFSET / MIRROR) are CYCLES-only and are refused on any other type rather than ignored. REPEAT_OFFSET is the one you want for a walk cycle or anything that should accumulate rather than snap back.

Modifiers are COUNTED off the curves before and after, because fcurve.modifiers.new returns an object whether or not it stuck. countsAgree is that arithmetic checked rather than asserted.

A MODIFIER EXISTING IS NOT THE SAME AS IT HAVING AN EFFECT. To prove a loop is live, sample past the last keyframe with bl_evaluate_at_frame - that reads through the depsgraph, so it sees the modifier where every raw property read does not.
bl_list_actions:
Every action in the file, who uses it, and whether it will survive a save.

THE FIELD TO READ IS willBeDeletedOnSave. An action with no users and no fake user is removed the next time the file is written - silently, and by the save SUCCEEDING. It is the same purge bl_save_file reports as purgedOrphans, seen from the other side, and an action is the easiest thing in Blender to leave in that state: unlink it from one object and it is already there.

usedBy is built by walking objects rather than by asking the action. An action knows its user COUNT and not their names, while 'which object is this clip on' is the question anybody actually has.

ACTION NAMES ARE CLIP NAMES. glTF and FBX write them into the engine, so an auto-generated Action.003 becomes a string somebody downstream has to live with and cannot easily change. Each row also carries curve and keyframe counts and the frame range.
bl_create_action:
Create a named action, optionally assigning it to an object.

NAMING IS THE ENTIRE POINT. An object gets whatever Blender auto-named its action, and that string is what glTF and FBX write into the engine as the clip name - so every clip exported through this bridge arrived downstream named after nothing. Nothing here could set it.

fake_user DEFAULTS TRUE. A freshly created, unassigned action has zero users by definition, so without a fake user it would be deleted by the next save. Where a default can either lose work or keep it, this one keeps it.

nameWasTaken is reported because Blender uniquifies silently: ask for 'Walk' when one exists and you get 'Walk.001', and a caller who then looks up 'Walk' finds a DIFFERENT action, or none.
bl_assign_action:
Put an existing action on an object, or clear it.

An object held ONE action forever. bl_set_keyframe creates one on first use and nothing could swap it, so a second clip on the same rig was impossible without deleting the first.

CLEARING IS THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION. An unlinked action with no fake user drops to zero users and is deleted on the next save, so this reports previousSurvivesSave - read AFTER the unlink, because the user count is exactly what the unlink changed. Give it a fake user first if you want to keep it.

The assignment is re-read off the object afterwards and the op refuses to claim success if it did not take, rather than trusting that setting the property worked.
bl_set_bone_pose:
Pose a bone on an armature. Character animation had zero coverage here - bones could be listed and renamed and nothing else.

It was also unreachable through bl_set_keyframe until the same day: that op's dotted-path walk stripped subscripts, so pose.bones["hand"].location resolved to the bone COLLECTION and the write failed while the keyframe still landed, holding the old value.

ROTATION MODE IS CHECKED, not assumed. A euler on a QUATERNION bone and a quaternion on a euler bone are both silently ignored by Blender. Both are refused here, as is passing the two together.

THE READ-BACK IS EVALUATED. A bone with an IK chain, a Copy Rotation or a Limit does NOT end up where you put it, and pose_bone.matrix is the raw value rather than the result. The response reports 'written' off the pose bone and 'evaluatedHeadWorld' / 'evaluatedTailWorld' through the depsgraph. If those differ, that is the constraint doing its job rather than a fault, and the constraints list names which one. Reporting only what you wrote back at you would be a proxy that cannot fail.
bl_set_shape_key:
Set a shape key's influence, and optionally its slider range. The write half of bl_list_shape_keys, which could only read.

THE RANGE IS APPLIED BEFORE THE VALUE. Setting a value outside the OLD range would be clamped to it and then look wrong even though the new range allows it - an ordering that matters and is easy to get backwards.

BLENDER CLAMPS SILENTLY. Asking for 2.0 on a 0..1 key leaves 1.0 and reports nothing at all, so the response carries requestedValue alongside the actual value and a 'clamped' flag naming the difference. Otherwise it is found later, in a render, as a shape that did not go as far as it was told to.
bl_bake_to_keyframes:
Bake evaluated motion into REAL keyframes that an exporter will carry.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. bl_bake_physics bakes POINT CACHES, and no exporter reads them - not FBX, not glTF. So a rigid-body simulation authored through this bridge could be rendered here and handed to nothing at all. Constraints and drivers have the same problem one step removed: they evaluate correctly in Blender and export as a STATIC object, because an exporter writes keyframes and a constraint is not one.

THE POSTCONDITION IS THE MOTION, NOT THE KEY COUNT. The evaluated world matrix is sampled across the range BEFORE the bake and again after, and maxPositionError, maxRotationErrorRadians and motionPreserved report whether the movement survived. Producing the right NUMBER of keyframes while losing the motion is the normal failure when visual keying is off, and no count of keys can see it.

The probe frames are spread across the range rather than taken from one end, because a bake that loses the motion still matches at the first frame, where the object has not moved yet.

visual_keying defaults TRUE. With it off the bake records the object's OWN transform and discards everything a constraint or a simulation was contributing, which is precisely how this goes wrong.

A SOURCE LEFT IN PLACE KEEPS EVALUATING ON TOP OF THE NEW KEYS. Constraints continue to apply unless clear_constraints is passed, and an object whose rigid body is still active is still driven by the simulation with its new keyframes ignored - remove_rigid_body handles that. hadConstraints and hadRigidBody report what was there, so a caller can tell whether they needed either.
